chapters.title: Vanity of Vanities
chapters.html:
Ecclesiastes 1

1The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.

2"Vanity of vanities," says the Preacher, "vanity of vanities! All is vanity."

3What does a man gain from all his toil at which he toils under the sun?

4A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever.

5The sun rises, and the sun goes down, and pants back to its place, where it rises.

6The wind goes to the south and turns around to the north; around and around goes the wind, and on its rounds the wind returns.

7All the streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full; to the place where the streams flow, there they flow again.

8All things are full of weariness; no one can utter it. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.

9What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun.

10Is there a thing of which it is said, "See, this is new"? It has been already, in the ages before us.

11There is no remembrance of those who came before, and of those who are yet to come there will be no remembrance among those who come after them.

12I the Preacher have been king over Israel in Jerusalem.

13I set my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven. It is an unhappy business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.

14I have seen all the works that are done under the sun, and indeed, all is vanity and a chasing after wind.

15What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is lacking cannot be counted.

16I said in my heart, "I have grown great and added wisdom beyond all who were over Jerusalem before me, and my heart has seen much wisdom and knowledge."

17So I set my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly. I came to know that this also is a chasing after wind.

18For in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.

Notes

  • v1 "the Preacher" — Qohelet, "one who gathers," the speaker to an assembly (qahal); the Greek Ekklesiastes gives the book its name. "Son of David, king in Jerusalem" points to Solomon, though the book never names him.

  • v2 "Vanity" — hevel, the word that was Abel's name (Genesis 4:2). There it names a man; here it is a word in the sentence.

  • v2 "Vanity of vanities" — the Hebrew way of saying "the utmost vanity," like "holy of holies." Hevel is literally a breath or vapor, and it is "vanity" every time in this book.

  • v3 "under the sun" — the book's phrase for life as seen from this world, about thirty times.

  • vv4–7 — the sun, the wind and the streams go round and round and arrive nowhere.

  • v5 "pants back to its place" — sho'ef, panting like a runner.

  • v14 "a chasing after wind" — re'ut ruach, wind, not spirit; the phrase returns through chapter 6. In v17 it is ra'yon ruach, the same sense.

  • v15 "What is crooked cannot be made straight" — as in 7:13.

chapters.title: I Hated All My Toil
chapters.html:
Ecclesiastes 2

1I said in my heart, "Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy what is good." But this also was vanity.

2I said of laughter, "It is madness," and of pleasure, "What does it do?"

3I searched in my heart how to cheer my body with wine — my heart still guiding me with wisdom — and how to lay hold of folly, until I might see what was good for the children of man to do under heaven during the few days of their life.

4I made great works: I built houses for myself; I planted vineyards for myself.

5I made myself gardens and parks and planted in them all kinds of fruit trees.

6I made myself pools of water from which to water a forest of growing trees.

7I bought male and female servants, and had servants born in my house. I also had great possessions of herds and flocks, more than any who had been before me in Jerusalem.

8I also gathered for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I got singers, men and women, and the delights of the children of man — many concubines.

9So I became great and surpassed all who were before me in Jerusalem. My wisdom also remained with me.

10Whatever my eyes asked for I did not keep from them. I kept my heart from no pleasure, for my heart found pleasure in all my toil, and this was my portion from all my toil.

11Then I turned to all the works that my hands had done and to the toil I had spent in doing them, and indeed, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no gain under the sun.

12So I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly. For what can the man do who comes after the king? Only what has already been done.

13Then I saw that there is more gain in wisdom than in folly, as there is more gain in light than in darkness.

14The wise man has his eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I perceived that one fate befalls them all.

15So I said in my heart, "What befalls the fool will befall me also. Why then have I been so very wise?" I said in my heart that this also is vanity.

16For of the wise as of the fool there is no remembrance forever, since in the days to come all will long be forgotten. How the wise dies just like the fool!

17So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a chasing after wind.

18I hated all my toil at which I toil under the sun, since I must leave it to the man who will come after me,

19and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all for which I toiled and used my wisdom under the sun. This also is vanity.

20So I turned and gave my heart up to despair over all the toil at which I had toiled under the sun,

21because there is a man whose toil is done with wisdom and knowledge and skill, and he must leave it as a portion to a man who did not toil for it. This also is vanity and a great evil.

22What does a man get from all his toil and the striving of his heart at which he toils under the sun?

23For all his days are pain, and his business is vexation; even at night his heart does not rest. This also is vanity.

24There is nothing better for a man than to eat and drink and let his soul see good in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God,

25for who can eat or who can have enjoyment apart from me?

26For to the man who is good in His sight He has given wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner He has given the business of gathering and collecting, only to give to the one who is good in God's sight. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.

Notes

  • vv1–11 — the king's experiment: pleasure, wine, building, gardens, servants, treasure, music. He had everything, and found "no gain under the sun."

  • v8 "many concubines" — shiddah veshiddot, words found only here; the meaning is uncertain, and "chests" or "cupbearers" have been proposed.

  • v12 "what can the man do who comes after the king?" — no successor can go further; the line is hard in the Hebrew.

  • v14 "one fate" — miqreh, what happens, chance, here death, which comes to wise and fool alike (3:19; 9:2–3).

  • v20 "gave my heart up to despair" — leya'esh, to give up hope.

  • v24 "There is nothing better for a man than to eat and drink" — the first of the book's refrains of simple joy (3:12–13, 22; 5:18; 8:15; 9:7), received as a gift "from the hand of God."

  • v25 "apart from me" — the Hebrew is followed: who can enjoy more than the Preacher could? The Greek and some Hebrew manuscripts read "apart from Him."

  • v26 "the one who is good in His sight… the sinner" — "sinner" (chote) may mean one who misses the mark, the one God does not favor.

chapters.title: A Time for Everything
chapters.html:
Ecclesiastes 3

1For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:

2a time to be born, and a time to die;
a time to plant, and a time to uproot what is planted;

3a time to kill, and a time to heal;
a time to break down, and a time to build up;

4a time to weep, and a time to laugh;
a time to mourn, and a time to dance;

5a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together;
a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;

6a time to seek, and a time to lose;
a time to keep, and a time to cast away;

7a time to tear, and a time to sew;
a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;

8a time to love, and a time to hate;
a time for war, and a time for peace.

9What gain has the worker from that at which he toils?

10I have seen the business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.

11He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also put eternity in their hearts, yet so that man cannot find out the work that God has done from beginning to end.

12I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and to do good as long as they live;

13and also that every man should eat and drink and see good in all his toil — it is the gift of God.

14I know that whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it. God has done it, so that people fear before Him.

15What is, already has been; what is to be, already has been; and God seeks what has been driven away.

16Moreover, I saw under the sun: in the place of justice, there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, there was wickedness.

17I said in my heart, "God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every work there."

18I said in my heart concerning the children of man: God is testing them, so that they may see that they themselves are beasts.

19For what befalls the children of man and what befalls the beasts is one and the same; as one dies, so dies the other. They all have one breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts, for all is vanity.

20All go to one place. All are from the dust, and all return to the dust.

21Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?

22So I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his works, for that is his portion. Who can bring him to see what will be after him?

Notes

  • vv2–8 — fourteen pairs of opposites, every human act given its time; God holds the times (v11; Psalm 31:15).

  • v5 "a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together" — perhaps clearing a field and building a wall, or, as later readers took it, a picture of the marriage bed beside "a time to embrace."

  • v11 "He has also put eternity in their hearts" — ha'olam, "eternity" or "the world": a sense of what lies beyond time, yet no grasp of the whole.

  • v15 "God seeks what has been driven away" — nirdaf, "the pursued": God brings back what has passed, or God takes the side of the pursued.

  • vv19–21 "one breath… the spirit of man… the spirit of the beast" — ruach each time; the breath of life that people and animals share (Genesis 7:22). Lowercase, since it is not God's Spirit.

  • v20 "All are from the dust, and all return to the dust" — Genesis 3:19.

  • v21 "Who knows" — the Preacher does not deny a difference; he says no one under the sun can see it. 12:7 gives his answer: the spirit returns to God who gave it.

chapters.title: Two Are Better Than One
chapters.html:
Ecclesiastes 4

1Again I saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun. There were the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them. On the side of their oppressors there was power, and they had no one to comfort them.

2So I praised the dead who are already dead more than the living who are still alive.

3But better than both is he who has not yet been, who has not seen the evil work that is done under the sun.

4Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.

5The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh.

6Better is one hand full of quietness than two hands full of toil and a chasing after wind.

7Again I saw vanity under the sun:

8one man who has no other, neither son nor brother, yet there is no end to all his toil, and his eyes are never satisfied with riches. "For whom am I toiling and depriving my soul of good?" This also is vanity and an unhappy business.

9Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil.

10For if they fall, one will lift up his companion. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has no one to lift him up!

11Again, if two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone?

12Though a man may overpower one who is alone, two will stand against him — and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

13Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knows how to take warning.

14For he came out of prison to reign, though in his kingdom he had been born poor.

15I saw all the living who walk under the sun, with that second youth who would stand in his place.

16There was no end of all the people, of all those whom he led. Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.

Notes

  • v1 "they had no one to comfort them" — said twice, as the Hebrew does.

  • v5 "eats his own flesh" — the idle man destroys himself; v6 gives the balance between laziness and endless toil.

  • v8 "his eyes" — the read form, singular eino; the written form plural. The Hebrew moves into the man's own question without "he says."

  • vv9–12 — the worth of a companion, at work, in a fall, in the cold, against an attacker; "a threefold cord," where two become three.

  • vv13–16 — a story of a youth who rose from prison to the throne and was forgotten in turn; the Hebrew does not say who.

  • v16 and Hebrew 4:17 — the Hebrew counts one more verse in this chapter; the English numbering, which begins chapter 5 with it, is followed, so it is rendered as 5:1.
